source.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities

page_placements.theme: Cross-seed and cross-model universality is linked to unit interpretability
Units mix features without capacity pressure

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether learned representations are axis-aligned or mixed using synthetic supervised-learning experiments and an alignment measure, rather than the original neuron-response measurement.
record.gate_note: The synthetic experiments measure latent-to-neuron axis alignment, which bears on V4 and V5. The real-model and macaque analyses report associations between interpretability scores and cross-system unit matches, not whether an individual unit responds to unrelated inputs; these are recorded under fits_no_version. Results on undercomplete encoders' KL loss and linear versus nonlinear encoding do not measure unit-level polysemanticity and are not rows.
record.test_reason: In exact-capacity toy encoders (m = n′, five latents), the study measures per-neuron axis alignment (MCC) across output activation, data distribution, weight decay and seeds. This bears on whether mixed-selectivity (polysemantic) neurons arise when there are enough neurons for every feature (V4), and how their share depends on activation and regularization (V5). The real-model and macaque MIS–MMU analyses measure cross-system matching, not polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that with too few dimensions (m < n′) the optimal encoder is nonlinear and not identifiable. Also add that in the discriminative setting sparse latents plus the spark condition allow sparse-dictionary recovery from polysemantic codes, which the authors offer as an explanation of SAE success.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops identifiability theory and uses synthetic latent-recovery experiments and interpretability-score analyses; it does not reproduce the original neuron-response analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Axis alignment changes with the DGP, output activation, weight decay, conditional-entropy variation and readout type, conditional dependence, marginal family, signed-latent rate, and output activation relaxation.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-neuron MIS positively predicts cross-model MMU for all 12 vision-model pairs, and more weakly for LLMs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More interpretable units more often have a correlated counterpart in another model.

fits_no_version.finding: MIS–MMU correlations between two macaques are positive but not significant (r = 0.158, p = 0.0986; r = 0.135, p = 0.312).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More interpretable IT neurons tend to have cross-subject counterparts; the evidence is weak.

fits_no_version.finding: At exact capacity with weight decay, the data distribution drives mixing: signed latents (MCC 0.770 at p = 0.1, 0.049 at p = 0.5) and log-normal marginals (0.668) break alignment; Gamma, Weibull and copula 0.5 do not (0.990, 0.984, 0.968).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether neurons become monosemantic at full capacity depends on latent sign support and distribution shape.

record.problems: The theoretical claims rely on idealized assumptions, including a specified sparse generative process and global optimality. The synthetic experiments use ten random seeds; some reported alignment outcomes are figure-only. The authors note initialization dependence, slow convergence, and sensitivity to violations of non-negative latent support and other assumptions. The real-data analysis uses MIS as a proxy for disentanglement and does not directly observe true latents.
record.rows_left_out: Undercomplete encoder KL results and linear-versus-MLP comparisons in Sections 5.2 and 9.2 were left out because they measure prediction loss and encoder linearity, not unit-level polysemanticity. Linear-alignment results from Section 5.1 and the assumption ablations were not added as separate rows where they do not measure axis alignment.

untested.parts: No test of individual vision-model neurons responding to unrelated images.
No share of LLM MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens, and no layer comparison.
The undercomplete and compressed-sensing experiments measure KL, encoder linearity and latent recovery, not per-neuron polysemanticity caused by packing.
Training noise as a distinct cause is not tested; regularization is tested only as weight decay; real networks are not tested.
SoLU, modern convnets and architecture beyond readout/output activation are not tested. Task performance or loss cost of the changes is not reported.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
Activation-range coverage and explanation scoring are not varied.

missing.what: Seed-level trajectories with zero weight decay at 10^6 updates for the hyperspherical and linear-output conditions (figure only). These show whether the r1–r3 mixing persists with a longer budget.
Exp+BN output activation results improving axis alignment versus ReLU, and the power-spectrum correlate of convergence.

record.verdict_notes: The record's row states measured axis alignment (monosemanticity), the inverse of the claim. All V4/V5 states are re-expressed as polysemantic mixing present. For V5, the evidence lies in cross-row contrasts, not single rows. The main-text Figure 1 runs use 50k steps; the supplement ablations use 10^6 steps with weight decay 0.03, so r1–r4 and r17–r18 are not directly comparable. The authors caution that the ablations do not test whether each assumption is necessary.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether individual vision-model neurons respond to unrelated image inputs, including the cited InceptionV1 neuron.
It does not measure the share of language-model MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or compare that share across layers.

The undercomplete-capacity experiments measure prediction loss and encoder linearity, not whether excess features are packed into individual polysemantic neurons or whether superposition causes that packing.

Tests initialization sensitivity and weight-decay effects on axis alignment in an exact-capacity synthetic setting; it does not test training noise as a distinct cause or establish that every feature has a dedicated neuron in real networks.

Tests synthetic output activations and regularization, and relaxations of the study's generative assumptions. It does not test SoLU, modern convnets, or whether the changes preserve performance at a stated cost.
The study does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons with better explanations to determine whether their unrelated responses share a feature.
It does not vary activation-range coverage or explanation-scoring methods to test measurement dependence.

source_check.notes: The study measures MCC axis alignment of five synthetic latents in exact-capacity encoders, not neuron responses in trained networks. Its real-network MIS-MMU analyses (r20, r21) bear on no version. 'Converges' for r4 is eventual: at 10^6 updates without weight decay only 3/10 seeds reach MCC 0.90 (r5). The '106' update counts in rows r5-r8 mean 10^6.

statements.correction: r4: sparse DGP + ReLU output, no weight decay (base setting, line 1915; Sec 5.1 defers weight-decay effects to 9.1); converges slowly to axis alignment; only 3/10 seeds reach MCC >= 0.90 by 10^6 updates (r5). Weight decay 0.01: median MCC 0.993, 9/10 >= 0.90 (r7); 0.03: median 0.987, 10/10 (r8).
statements.problem: r4 (slow convergence to axis alignment) is a no-weight-decay result. The statement's conditions (weight decay >= 0.01) and its weight-decay headline wrongly cover it.

statements.correction: arXiv:2610.20851 varies output activation at exact capacity: with a sparse DGP and no weight decay, linear output retains mixed selectivity and ReLU converges slowly to axis alignment (r3 vs r4). Under weight decay 0.03: ReLU 0.994, LeakyReLU 0.987, linear 0.968 MCC (r17, r18). Layer norm and other regularizers are untested.
statements.problem: The line about this study (regularization tested only as weight decay) is right. But listing activation nonlinearities as untested ignores this study's output-activation test at exact capacity, which the synthesis itself cites in V4.wording_issues[1].

statements.correction: Contrast holds only with the sparse non-negative exponential DGP, m = n', no weight decay (r3 vs r4). With a hyperspherical DGP, both linear and ReLU outputs retain mixed selectivity (r1, r2). ReLU convergence is slow: 3/10 seeds reach MCC >= 0.90 by 10^6 updates (r5).
statements.problem: The linear-vs-ReLU contrast is stated without the sparse DGP condition. With a hyperspherical DGP, ReLU output also retains mixed selectivity (r2).
